title: The ten-day course
hookLine: S. N. Goenka's ten-day silent courses in the method of U Ba Khin, offered on donations

cards: At the front desk you hand over your phone. Your books go too, and your notebook, and your pen. Someone shows you to a simple room and a cushion in a quiet hall.

For the next ten days you won't talk with the person on the next cushion, or catch their eye, or pass them a note. You'll sit, eat plain food, walk, sleep, and sit again. And at the end, nobody hands you a bill.
People sign up for this, again and again.

teach.h: FROM U BA KHIN TO GOENKA.

teach.b: Goenka was born into an Indian family in Burma, now Myanmar, and became a businessman there. He learned meditation from U Ba Khin, a Burmese lay teacher who also served in his country's government.

Goenka later began teaching in India, and the courses spread to centers around the world, taught in the same form in each place, with his recorded instructions guiding the students. Second, the silence.
The courses ask for noble silence: no speaking, gestures or messages between students, so each person is left alone with their own mind.
A student may still speak with the teacher about the practice, and with the staff about practical needs. Third, the method.

teach.h: FIRST THE BREATH, THEN THE BODY.
teach.b: It begins with the breath, attention resting on the small area around the nostrils, feeling the air come and go.
When the mind has steadied, attention moves through the whole body, part by part: warmth, pressure, tingling, ache.
The instruction is to observe without grasping the pleasant or pushing away the unpleasant, and to see that each sensation arises and passes. The Pali word for that passing is anicca, impermanence.

On the final day comes metta, loving kindness, and the silence lifts. Goenka presented the method as belonging to no sect, something anyone could try without converting. Fourth, the money, or the lack of it.
There's no charge for teaching, food or lodging.
Courses run on donations from people who have finished one and want someone else to have the same chance.
Every student sits, in a sense, as the guest of a stranger who came before.

how: Students at S. N. Goenka's courses keep noble silence for ten days, practicing attention to the breath and then to sensations throughout the body; the courses charge no fee and are funded by donations from past students.

games.q: it's the middle of the course. your knee aches and a pleasant warmth spreads through your hands. what does the method ask?
o: chase the warmth and ignore the knee.
observe both, grasping at neither, and see each one pass.
stop sitting until the ache is gone.
games.why: observe without grasping or pushing away. the point is to see that every sensation arises and passes: anicca.

practice: Sit upright with your eyes closed, and rest attention on the small area just below the nostrils, above the upper lip, feeling the breath touch there, natural, as it is. When the mind wanders, come back without scolding yourself.
Near the end, let attention move once, slowly, from the top of the head down to the toes, noticing whatever sensation is there and letting it pass.

orig.note: Pali anicca, impermanence: what the ten-day course asks students to see in every sensation.
